at.step: Map applies a function to each input record independently, emitting key-value pairs. The shuffle moves every pair to the reduce task that owns its key, by a partition function — the key’s hash, taken modulo the reduce-task count, by default. Reduce is called once per key with every value that landed there.

The map function emits each word plus a count of one; the reduce function sums every count that arrives for the same word. Map and reduce are each embarrassingly parallel — the exchange in between is the one step where every map task talks to every reduce task.

Each phase, alone, has a span of one task — the work-span lesson already given. The shuffle is different: it is the step that forces every map task’s output toward every reduce task that might own a piece of it, and that all-to-all exchange is what a MapReduce job actually pays for.

syllabus.clause: combiners and the associativity/commutativity they require

at.step: When a reduce function is commutative and associative, it may run early — on one map task’s own output, before the exchange — merging duplicate keys into one record per map task instead of one record per occurrence. A common word, following a Zipf distribution, makes this collapse dramatic.

The same word count, shuffled with and without a combiner: far fewer records cross the network with one, and both runs land on the identical final answer — a combiner changes how much moves, never what the answer is, when the algebra actually holds.

A combiner’s output must combine further, in any grouping and in any order, because the framework decides neither how work splits among map tasks nor what order partial results arrive in. That is exactly associativity and commutativity — not a convenience, a requirement.

A concrete example settles it: three groups’ own means, averaged, land far from the true pooled mean. The fix combines sum-and-count pairs instead of means, and divides only once, in the final reduce — a combinable representation exists even when the obvious one does not.

syllabus.clause: round complexity in the MPC model

at.step: A round is one local computation phase followed by one all-to-all exchange. The Massively Parallel Communication model counts exactly two things: how many rounds a computation takes, and the most data any one server receives in any round — nothing about an actual framework’s engineering enters the cost at all.

A two-relation join finishes in one round with no replication, by partitioning on the shared join column. A three-relation join among the same kind of relations needs real replication to finish in that same one round — the query’s own shape, not its size, decides the replication needed.

A chain of dependent steps needs a number of rounds that grows with the chain’s own length, under any scheme that only doubles its reach each round — no fixed round count, however many servers help, changes that.

syllabus.clause: mapping back to joins and aggregations

at.step: A reduce-side equi-join is map-with-a-tag, shuffle on the join key, reduce emitting the matching pairs for each key — the same partitioning idea a hash join used on one machine’s memory, now applied across a network. A skewed key sending most of its records to one reducer is the same hot-partition problem, paid for in network time instead of disk time.
